e1.reasoning: Featured diegetic use of a recognizable hit song for 12 seconds with character interaction. Ringgold forecloses de minimis for deliberately featured works; § 504(c) exposure covers two separate copyrights. License both sync and master before any distribution, or cut/replace the cue.

briefs.argument: This is a 12-second, plot-integral use of a major-label hit — characters react to the song, making it a featured sync use. Unlicensed sync and master use exposes the production to statutory damages of up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement, and both the composition (UMPG) and the master (XO/Republic) are implicated as separate works. There is no realistic de-minimis position: courts reject de-minimis where the copyrighted work is deliberately featured and recognizable. Distribution without a license is uninsurable.

precedents.holding: Statutory damages up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement, without proof of actual harm.
precedents.relevance: Two works (composition + master) are in play; willfulness is easy to show for a knowing sync use.

precedents.holding: Recognizable, deliberately included copyrighted work in a TV scene was not de minimis and infringed.
precedents.relevance: A deliberately featured, recognizable work defeats a de-minimis defense.
precedents.quote: The de minimis doctrine is inapplicable where the copying is qualitatively and quantitatively significant enough that the ordinary observer would recognize the appropriation.

briefs.argument: The use is diegetic — the song plays from a character's phone within the story world, not as underscore. But candor requires conceding: diegetic use is still a use requiring sync and master licenses; the doctrine offers no exemption for source music, and the 12-second duration with on-screen character reaction makes the work a focal element. The defense has no precedent to stand on at this prominence.

precedents.holding: Fleeting, out-of-focus, unidentifiable background use of copyrighted works was de minimis.
precedents.relevance: Cited for contrast: this use is the opposite — clear, extended, and plot-integral.

e2.reasoning: Incidental background depiction of a consumer product in an expressive work is well protected (Rogers; Caterpillar) and Coca-Cola's enforcement posture toward film depiction is cooperative. Defensible as-is; a free placement agreement would convert the residual risk to zero if the producer prefers.

briefs.argument: The can sits on the kitchen table for six seconds at 60% centrality — visible enough to read the script mark. While depiction alone is rarely actionable, the conservative path for E&O purposes is either a product-placement agreement (often free — Coca-Cola actively places product) or a two-second art-department swap to a greeked can.

precedents.holding: Deliberate set-dressing with protected material can be actionable where recognizable.
precedents.relevance: Cited by analogy for deliberate set-dressing, though trademark (not copyright) governs here.

briefs.argument: An ordinary soda can on a kitchen table is precisely the realistic incidental depiction courts protect in expressive works. There is no plot role, no disparagement, and no suggestion of sponsorship — under Rogers and Caterpillar, trademark owners cannot control truthful depictions of their products existing in the world. Productions depict branded consumer goods constantly without licenses.

precedents.holding: Trademark use in expressive works is protected absent artistic irrelevance or explicit misleading.
precedents.relevance: Incidental prop depiction has artistic relevance (realism) and implies no sponsorship.

precedents.case_name: Caterpillar Inc. v. Walt Disney Co.
precedents.holding: Depiction of branded products in film, without more, is not trademark infringement.
precedents.relevance: Directly on point for a background consumer product.

e3.reasoning: The Rogers defense is legally strong for wardrobe depiction, but prominence (15s, lead actor, two scenes) plus Nike's documented enforcement posture makes the practical calculus close: an $800/shot blur is cheaper than answering Nike's first letter. Escalate to counsel with a recommendation to blur or change wardrobe unless the depiction carries deliberate artistic weight.

briefs.argument: The Swoosh appears for 15 seconds across two scenes on the lead actor at 12% frame coverage — this is prominence, not incident. Nike operates one of the most aggressive trademark enforcement programs in existence and moved for a TRO within days in the MSCHF matter. Even where a defense ultimately prevails, Nike's demonstrated willingness to litigate makes the expected cost of a dispute far exceed the cost of a wardrobe blur. Prominent, repeated display on a protagonist also edges toward implied endorsement, weakening the expressive-use defense.

precedents.case_name: Nike, Inc. v. MSCHF Product Studio, Inc.
precedents.holding: Nike obtained rapid injunctive relief against unauthorized use of its marks on modified products.
precedents.relevance: Demonstrates enforcement speed and appetite, which drives practical risk regardless of the merits.

briefs.argument: Trademarks appearing in expressive works enjoy robust First Amendment protection: under Rogers, use of a mark in an expressive work is actionable only if it has no artistic relevance or explicitly misleads about sponsorship. A character wearing ordinary branded streetwear is realistic set dressing with artistic relevance and no sponsorship claim. Courts have repeatedly refused to let trademark owners control depictions of their products in film.

precedents.holding: Trademark use in expressive works is protected unless artistically irrelevant or explicitly misleading.
precedents.relevance: Wardrobe depiction in a narrative film sits squarely inside the Rogers safe harbor.
precedents.quote: The [Lanham] Act should be construed to apply to artistic works only where the public interest in avoiding consumer confusion outweighs the public interest in free expression.

precedents.case_name: Caterpillar Inc. v. Walt Disney Co.
precedents.holding: Court refused to enjoin depiction of Caterpillar bulldozers as villainous machinery in a film.
precedents.relevance: Mere depiction of branded products in a film, even unflattering, is not infringement.

e4.reasoning: This sits between Ringgold and Sandoval, but closer to Ringgold: the poster is in focus, framed as decor, and identifiable at 20% coverage. With a $500–$5k license band and a cooperative rights holder, clearing is cheap relative to the litigation-anchored downside. License it, or reframe/soften focus so Sandoval controls.

briefs.argument: Ringgold is directly on point and fatal: a copyrighted poster visible in the background of a scene for a comparable duration (26.75 seconds aggregate in Ringgold; 5 continuous seconds at 20% frame coverage here, in focus) was held infringing, with the Second Circuit explicitly rejecting a de-minimis defense where the work is recognizable and its expressive content is conveyed. The poster is framed, lit, and identifiable — its expressive value is being used as set decoration without license.

precedents.holding: A poster of a copyrighted artwork visible in a TV scene background was infringing; de minimis rejected.
precedents.relevance: Nearly identical fact pattern: decorative poster, background of a dramatic scene, recognizable.
precedents.quote: The painting component of the poster is recognizable as a painting, and with sufficient observable detail for the average lay observer to discern African-Americans wearing hats and colorful clothing.

briefs.argument: Sandoval shows the line: where background works are fleeting, obscured, or unidentifiable, the use is de minimis. At five seconds with actors in the foreground pulling focus, an average observer's ability to discern the poster's protected expression is genuinely contestable — the observability analysis, not raw duration, controls. A licensing conversation at the $500–$5k band is nonetheless cheap certainty.

precedents.holding: Background photographs that were fleeting and out of focus were de minimis and non-infringing.
precedents.relevance: The counter-anchor: if the poster reads as unidentifiable set dressing, no infringement.

e5.reasoning: Prominent use of an enforceable copyrighted work whose owner cannot be identified is the single worst clearance posture — no license is even possible yet. Escalate: commission a human investigation to identify the artist (local arts orgs, street-art registries, the building owner), and prepare the fallback of recutting the shot to Sandoval territory.

briefs.argument: The mural fills 30% of frame for six seconds as the walking shot's backdrop — it is the shot's visual subject, not incident. Murals are fully copyright-protected pictorial works, and street artists have repeatedly and successfully enforced against commercial exploitation of their work in media. Because deep research could not identify the artist, the production faces the worst posture: a live copyright with an untraceable owner. E&O underwriters treat unidentifiable rights holders as uninsurable exposure, and VARA adds moral-rights complications no release can cure retroactively.

precedents.holding: A muralist's copyright claim over commercial photography featuring his mural survived summary judgment.
precedents.relevance: Street art is enforceable copyright; prominent commercial use of murals draws real claims.

precedents.holding: Authors of works of visual art hold attribution and integrity rights independent of copyright ownership.
precedents.relevance: Even a later license from a building owner would not extinguish the artist's own rights.

briefs.argument: The mural is public street context in a walking shot — filming the world as it exists. If the shot were brief or the mural incidental, Sandoval-style observability arguments would apply. But at 30% coverage for six seconds the work's expression is plainly conveyed, and candor requires acknowledging that the de-minimis position is weak on these facts. The stronger practical defense is mitigation: reframe, shorten, or defocus the shot.

precedents.holding: Fleeting, unidentifiable background use is de minimis.
precedents.relevance: Would control only if the shot were recut to make the mural incidental.
